newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Lack of competition limits Ivorian base rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: Lack of competition limits Ivorian base rate cuts.

text.p: Base lending rates in Ivory Coast have been falling since the start of August because the leading banks are stuffed full of money, but the reductions will be minimal as long as competition remains limited, bankers said.

SGBCI, part of France's Societe Generale, announced on August 1 that it had cut its base rate to 9.00 percent from 9.50 percent, while state-controlled BIAO reduced its rate to 9.25 percent from 9.75 percent.

"They've got more money than they know what to do with. Unfortunately, the people that want the money are high risk," said an official at one of the smaller specialist banks, adding the big banks were in no hurry to compete for risky business.
Another banker highlighted the lack of competition in Ivory Coast, saying the market was sewn up by four big banks, three of them part of French groups.
The other two big players, in addition to SGBCI and BIAO, are SIB, part of Credit Lyonnais, and BICICI, controlled by Banque Nationale de Paris .
"There are four big banks and they do what they want. And the other banks are quite happy, because they get the big margins, too," the banker said.

He estimated that 50 percent of lending to clients was in the shape of formal loans and 50 percent through overdrafts. Rates on the latter were determined by base rates, and the banks were naturally content to keep these as high as possible, in the absence of competition for clients.
The recent fall in rates, however modest, will go some way to pleasing the authorities.
Ivory Coast is the powerhouse of the Economic and Monetary Union of West Africa (UEMOA), the West African bit of the Franc Zone, whose eight states share one currency, the CFA franc.
UEMOA's common central bank, the BCEAO, set a fixed rate of 4.00 percent on bills sold at its weekly money market tender on August 4, and stuck with the fixed rate on August 11.
That was down from a marginal rate at its previous tender on July 28 of 4.70 percent, and an average rate of 4.6410 percent.
Analysts interpreted the lower fixed rate as a signal to banks in the sub-region to cut their lending rates.
The central bank declined to comment, but BCEAO governor Charles Konan Banny has complained in recent weeks that bank credit was too dear.
"The BCEAO has been trying for three years to get base rates down. The problem is, they are doing it artificially, trying to impose it," one banker said.
As long as there is no real competition in the money markets, the central bank will have problems trying to get rates down through its tenders, bankers said.
Banny has regretted the fact that liquidity in the banking system was not finding its way into private sector investment.

Analysts blamed a lack of non-bank savings options, and said this would handicap the government's efforts to increase the savings ratio to 30 percent of GDP, in line with successful emerging economies in Asia, from around 14 percent now.

Share trading on the only bourse in the region, in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, is illiquid, and the few listed bonds rarely trade. A regional bourse is promised for the start of 1998, but analysts are sceptical about the timetable and say it will take years for it to be established as a conduit for savings.
